name: shopware
_readme: Shopware 6 as migration TARGET (Store API + Shopping Experiences, self-hosted / PaaS / SaaS) and as SOURCE (self-hosted or PaaS installation with custom plugins under custom/plugins). Seed from general platform knowledge; the as_source conventions are the standard Shopware 6 plugin/app anchors. Everything in research-seed.md is a hypothesis until verified with a developer.shopware.com / docs.shopware.com URL and a date. No adapter.py yet: a source scan needs one.

as_source.language_stack: PHP 8.x / Symfony (admin: Vue.js), MySQL/MariaDB, optional Elasticsearch/OpenSearch
as_source.default_frontend: Shopware Storefront (Twig + Bootstrap) with theme inheritance; optionally headless on the Store API
do_not_run: composer install / update against the client repository

snippets.version_markers: composer.lock -> the locked version of shopware/core (and shopware/administration, shopware/storefront, shopware/commercial for the Commercial plan); composer.json require constraints (shopware/core ^6.x) which are the INTENT, not the installed version; bin/console -V for the Symfony version only if a console output is provided; the plugin's own composer.json require on shopware/core gives the compatibility window per plugin, and each plugin's Migration*.php class-name timestamps show when it was last touched. Also check public/recovery or the update channel config for how the shop was updated. Never infer the running minor from composer.json alone - the lock file wins, and a PaaS/SaaS shop may run a newer patch than the repository suggests.
snippets.active_units_config: A plugin is ONLY active if its row in the `plugin` database table has active = 1 (and installed_at set) - that table is the authority, and it is NOT in the repository. So: a plugin folder present under custom/plugins or custom/static-plugins proves the code exists, not that it runs; a plugin present on disk but inactive (or never installed) in the DB is DEAD code that still costs review effort and can still break a build. Say this explicitly in any inventory: activation state is not derivable from the repository alone and must come from a `bin/console plugin:list` output, a DB dump or the merchant's confirmation. Supporting repository evidence: config/packages/*.yaml (bundle and Symfony configuration, feature flags), config/bundles.php in Symfony-style installations, the plugin's own composer.json extra.shopware-plugin-class, app manifest.xml (apps are registered per shop and also toggled outside the repository), theme.json for the active theme's inheritance, and any deployment recipe (deployment.yaml / CI pipeline) that lists which plugins are installed per environment.
snippets.package_sources: composer.json require of the root project and of every plugin (shopware/*, third-party vendors, Shopware Store packages resolved through packages.shopware.com), composer.lock for the resolved versions, custom/plugins/*/composer.json for partner and bespoke plugins, custom/apps/*/manifest.xml for apps, plus package.json / node_modules of storefront and administration bundles for JS dependencies.
snippets.override_mechanisms: overridden = the standard behaviour is replaced: Symfony DI service decoration (`decorates:` in services.xml, or the #[AsDecorator] attribute) - the `Decorated` class-name suffix is the community convention and a strong signal; replacing a service definition under the same service id; replacing an entry in a tagged collection (e.g. a cart processor/collector, a rule, a payment handler); a full Twig template override (same relative path under Resources/views/storefront/...) which hides the core template entirely. extended = added without replacing: event subscribers on entity events (EntityWrittenEvent, *.loaded, *.search.result.loaded) and business events (checkout.order.placed, ...), Twig `{% block %}` extension with `{% sw_extends %}` (adds to a core template instead of hiding it - the maintainable variant), entity extensions (EntityExtension adding fields/associations to a core entity), custom fields (data-only, configured in the admin, not in code), a new service consumed only by own code, scheduled tasks, and a new Store API route added next to the standard ones. shadowed / core-patch = a patched file under vendor/shopware (or a plugin autoloading a class in the Shopware\Core namespace): treat as core-patch, highest migration risk, and name the file. Distinguish Twig full override from sw_extends block extension in every finding - the effort and the upgrade risk differ by an order of magnitude.
snippets.schema_sources: custom/plugins/<Plugin>/src/Migration/Migration<timestamp><Name>.php (Doctrine-style migrations run by the plugin lifecycle; read update()/updateDestructive() and note destructive steps), EntityDefinition / EntityCollection / EntityEntity classes under src/Core/Content/... of the plugin (a new EntityDefinition = a new table; an EntityExtension = added fields on a core entity), custom field sets (defined in code via CustomFieldSetDefinition or created in the admin - the latter lives only in the DB), the `attributes`/`custom_fields` JSON columns on core entities, and any raw SQL in migrations or install lifecycle steps.
snippets.workflow_sources: Flow Builder: flows are DATA (the `flow` / `flow_sequence` tables, exported flow templates) plus code-side FlowAction / FlowEventAware classes and app flow actions in manifest.xml - so a flow can exist without any repository trace; say so. Rule Builder: rule conditions are DATA (`rule`, `rule_condition`) plus custom Rule classes registered with the `shopware.rule.definition` tag. State machines: the `order`, `order_transaction` and `order_delivery` state machines (`state_machine`, `state_machine_transition`) with their transition subscribers - custom states are typically created in a migration. Also scheduled tasks (ScheduledTask + ScheduledTaskHandler), message queue handlers (Symfony Messenger), and the legacy Business Events / mail templates.
snippets.data_script_sources: plugin install/activate lifecycle code writing demo or configuration data (Plugin::install / activate, EntityRepository upserts in migrations), fixture bundles, Admin API Sync API payloads (/api/_action/sync) used by integration scripts, import/export profiles (`import_export_profile` - mostly DB data, sometimes shipped as CSV mapping in the plugin), CSV mapping files under Resources/, and any deployment script that seeds config via bin/console system:config:set.
snippets.read_order: composer.json + composer.lock (root, then per plugin), custom/plugins|static-plugins listing and each plugin's composer.json extra.shopware-plugin-class, src/Resources/config/services.xml (DI: decorations, tags, subscribers), src/Migration/*, EntityDefinition and EntityExtension classes, src/Core|Storefront|Administration source, Resources/views/storefront (sw_extends vs. full override), Resources/app/administration (Vue overrides), Store API and Admin API route controllers, config/packages/*.yaml and config/services.yaml, custom/apps/*/manifest.xml, theme.json, then tests (intent only). Before asserting behaviour, state whether the plugin is active in the DB - if that is unknown, say so.
snippets.hosting_constraints: SHOPWARE CLOUD / SaaS ACCEPTS APPS ONLY - no PHP plugins at all. This is the single most important constraint: a source shop full of custom/plugins cannot move to SaaS without re-implementing each plugin as an app (manifest.xml, webhooks, app scripts, external app server) or dropping it. Consequences on SaaS: no filesystem persistence (no local file writes, media through the object store), no custom cron/console commands (only app-declared webhooks and Shopware's own scheduled tasks), no direct DB access and no raw SQL migrations, no Twig template overrides in the classic sense (app themes and app scripts only), no message-queue workers of your own, no Elasticsearch tuning. Shopware PaaS keeps plugins but still constrains the filesystem (ephemeral containers, object storage for media), build-time asset compilation, worker/cron configuration and outbound network policy. Self-hosted has none of these limits but carries the whole operations load. Always name WHICH deployment model a statement applies to - SaaS, PaaS or self-hosted.
snippets.api_families_hint: Store API for customer-facing operations, Admin API (incl. Sync API) for back office - see knowledge target_api_endpoint_families

as_target.default_frontend: Shopware Storefront (Twig) or headless on the Store API (Shopware Frontends / Vue Storefront)

snippets.critic2_persona: senior solution architect who has delivered many Shopware 6 projects, is a certified Shopware developer/architect, and knows exactly what is Community Edition, what is Commercial-plan gated (B2B Components, advanced search, custom pricing) and what only exists as a Store extension - across self-hosted, PaaS and SaaS
snippets.docs_domains: developer.shopware.com (developer documentation: plugin and app system, Store API and Admin API reference, DI/decoration, CMS data resolvers, Flow Builder and Rule Builder extension points, migration/upgrade guides, SaaS app-only constraints), docs.shopware.com (merchant/functional documentation incl. B2B Components and Commercial features), shopware.com/en/changelog and github.com/shopware/shopware releases (per-version changes and deprecations), store.shopware.com only to check whether a capability is really a paid third-party extension. State the exact minor (6.x.y) and the plan/edition for every feature claim - Commercial features are not in the open-source repository.
snippets.best_practice: extend, do not replace: service decoration and event subscribers over service replacement, `sw_extends` + Twig blocks over full template overrides, entity extensions or custom fields over new tables when the data belongs to a core entity; new tables only through plugin migrations with a non-destructive update() path; business logic in services behind an interface, thin controllers, Store API routes as the only customer-facing surface; use Rule Builder and Flow Builder for business logic that merchants must own - and add a custom Rule or FlowAction class instead of hard-coding the condition; never patch vendor/shopware; keep any capability that must survive a move to SaaS inside the app system rather than a PHP plugin.
snippets.critic2_focus: D1: version and edition facts - is the feature in 6.x standard, Commercial-plan only, or a Store extension; deprecation and removal notes per minor. D2: is the named standard counterpart a real Shopware service/entity/CMS element (name it), and is the classification consistent with Shopware extension best practice (decoration vs. subscriber vs. override). D3: does the Shopware standard really cover the requirement in the target minor AND in the chosen frontend (Storefront vs. headless on the Store API), and under which plan. D4: exact Store API route paths and their response shape, CMS element/block type names and whether a headless frontend renders them, Rule Builder / Flow Builder extension limits, and the deployment model (SaaS app-only) behind every statement.
snippets.expected_hotspots_d3: customer-specific and contract pricing driven by an ERP at request time (Rule Builder conditions cannot read live ERP data without a custom rule provider); live availability/ATP; B2B depth beyond B2B Components (multi-level approval chains, budgets per cost center, punchout OCI/cXML, quote negotiation rounds); configurable products and CPQ; complex bundle and set pricing; marketplace / multi-vendor operation; product data volumes needing Elasticsearch tuning; external identity (SSO/CIAM) for customer login; document generation beyond the standard invoice/delivery-note templates; and anything that must run on SaaS, where the answer changes because only apps are allowed.
snippets.expected_blockers_d4: Shopware Cloud/SaaS accepts apps only, so every PHP plugin in the source must be re-specified as an app or dropped; B2B Components and other Commercial features are plan-gated (name the plan and the price line); Rule Builder cannot evaluate live ERP data without a custom rule provider (and a custom rule class is not possible on SaaS); Store API coverage for B2B flows (employee/role management, approvals, quotes, shopping lists) is thinner than the Storefront and must be checked route by route; Flow Builder actions are a fixed catalogue plus custom/app actions, with no free scripting and limited error handling/retry semantics; full Twig template overrides have no headless equivalent - they must become frontend components; custom CMS element types need a data resolver plus a storefront (or headless) renderer; migration of custom entities and their DB-only configuration (flows, rules, custom field sets, import/export profiles) is data work, not code work.
snippets.content_model_notes: Shopping Experiences is the CMS: a cms_page has sections, sections have blocks, blocks contain elements (text, image, image-slider, product-box, product-slider, product-listing, form, html, video, ...). Layouts are assigned to categories, products and landing pages, so the same page type can render differently per sales channel. Everything a merchant builds is DATA in the cms_* tables - it does not appear in the repository, and it does not migrate with the code. Standard elements render out of the box in the Storefront; a CUSTOM element type needs three parts: an admin component (Vue), a CmsElementResolver (data resolver, PHP - or an app script on SaaS) and a storefront Twig template. Headless is the catch: a headless frontend gets the resolved CMS payload from /store-api/cms/* (or the page endpoints) as JSON and must implement a renderer per element type - nothing renders automatically, so every custom element and every Twig override in the source becomes frontend work. Custom fields extend entities without code but are only content-bearing if the frontend reads them explicitly.
